summary.title: Email explained from first principles
summary.one_liner: Learn how modern email works, from user-facing concepts like addresses and mailing lists to the architecture, SMTP protocols, message format, and security issues behind it.
takeaways: Email addresses have a local part and a domain part, and the standards allow far more characters than providers widely accept.
Subaddressing (user+tag@) and aliases are practical ways to filter mail, but subaddressing can be circumvented by spammers if the scheme is known.
Alias addresses forward mail and keep the original sender for replies, while mailing lists rewrite the envelope so replies go to the list administrator.
Email's architecture, protocols (such as SMTP), and message format are built on decades of RFCs, and the article explains why mail clients use outgoing servers.
summary.summary: This long article explains email from the user's perspective first, covering messages, mailbox providers, addresses, normalization, subaddressing, aliases, mailing lists, and address syntax under RFC 5322 and RFC 5321. It also covers the To, Cc, and Bcc recipient fields and common role-based addresses such as postmaster@. The author states that later chapters move on to the technical architecture, protocols, message format, and then privacy and security topics such as DANE, HSTS, S/MIME, and PGP. The page is written as a long-form reference with interactive tools and cites RFCs and real provider behavior throughout.
